title: Cutting-in, rolling and edge technique
audience: Painters who apply paint to finished standard and are paid for the higher-rate finishing work
learningOutcomes: Cut in edges and corners with a clean line and no lap marks.
Roll walls and ceilings with an even film that avoids roller marks and runs.
Plan a wet edge so that the paint is blended before it dries.

instruction.heading: Why application decides the finish
instruction.body: A room can have a good paint system and good preparation and still look poor because of how the paint was put on. The eye reads the edges, corners and junctions first, and it reads the wall as a whole under the light that falls across it. Cutting in and rolling are the two steps that set the finish. Cutting in is done with a brush before the roller covers the main area, and it defines the lines where walls meet ceilings, skirting, architraves, window frames and other surfaces. Rolling covers the open areas. Both steps are carried out in sections, and the aim is to join each section to the one before it while the paint is still workable. The technique here is general working practice, and the product data sheet for each paint takes priority over it on loading, drying and recoating.

instruction.heading: Cutting in and keeping a wet edge
instruction.body: Load the brush lightly. Dip only part of the bristles, and tap or wipe off the excess against the side of the tin so that the paint does not drip or build up at the ferrule. Draw the brush along the edge with a steady stroke, using the tip and part of the body of the brush, and keep the line straight by guiding the brush with the other hand or with an edging tool where the surface allows. Work in sections small enough to roll before the cut-in dries. The cut-in should still be wet when the roller reaches it, so that the roller blends the two without leaving a line. A dry edge that the roller meets is the usual cause of a lap mark, which is a dark or lighter band where the paint has dried at different rates. Keep the brush clean between strokes, and never load a dirty or clogged brush with fresh paint. Where a corner or junction is tight, cut in both sides before rolling the centre, so that the centre blends into two wet edges.

instruction.heading: Rolling for an even film
instruction.body: Load the roller evenly across its sleeve by rolling it in the tray until the nap is saturated but not dripping, and then roll off the excess on the tray's ridge. Start the roll at the edge of the section and roll out in a W or M pattern, so that paint is spread across the area. Once the area is covered, roll out in one direction, with the roller running from the wet edge into the previously finished area, with light pressure. Pressure does the work of spreading, not the roller's weight, so pressing hard forces paint out of the sleeve, leaves thick patches and causes runs and an uneven film. Work from the window or main light source toward the darker side of the room, so that any unevenness is seen while it is still wet. Use a sleeve whose nap suits the surface texture. A smooth sleeve on a textured wall leaves the texture uncovered, and a long-nap sleeve on a smooth wall can leave a heavy orange-peel finish. Keep the roller wet, and avoid rolling the same area repeatedly once the paint has started to tack, because overworking lifts the film and leaves marks.

instruction.heading: Finishing, inspection and correction
instruction.body: Inspect the finished wall and ceiling under a raking light, which is a light held low across the surface, because flat light hides marks that show clearly at a low angle. Look for lap marks, roller stipple, runs and sags, missed spots (holidays), brush marks at the edges, and any patch where the sheen differs. Correct a run or a lap mark while the paint is still wet, using the roller or the brush with light strokes, if the data sheet allows the product to be worked while wet. Do not keep rolling over a mark once it has started to dry, because the attempt to fix it usually makes it worse. Record defects that cannot be corrected, and do not claim that the finish is complete while a known defect is open.

instruction.heading: Working safely with brushes, rollers and ladders
instruction.body: Use a ladder or a platform that is stable and suited to the task, set up on a firm surface, and do not overreach. Keep the work area clear of trip hazards, with drop sheets secured so that they do not slide. Ventilate the room as the product's data sheet directs, and keep solvent-based products away from ignition sources. Clean brushes and rollers at the end of the day with the cleaner the product's data sheet names, and do not leave solvent-soaked rags in a pile, because they can heat up and ignite.

instruction.heading: Value, licence and what this lesson does not give
instruction.body: The licence test for painting work is set by the value of the job, not by the technique used to apply paint. A higher standard of finish does not change whether a licence is needed. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). The position for other states is set out in “Paint systems, primers and coverage” and “Painting quotes, variations and colour approval”. Completing this lesson does not give a painting licence, a certificate or any authority to undertake regulated building work.

procedure: Prepare the surface and protect the floor, fittings, switches and adjacent surfaces with drop sheets and masking.
Load the brush lightly, wipe off the excess, and cut in the edges and corners in short sections, keeping each cut-in wet.
Cut in both sides of any tight corner before rolling the centre of the section.
Load the roller evenly, and roll the section in a W or M pattern with light pressure.
Roll out in one direction, blending from the wet edge into the finished area, and keep the next section wet against the last.
Inspect the finish under a raking light, and correct any run or lap mark while the paint is still workable.
Clean the brushes and rollers at the end of the day with the cleaner the data sheet names, and dispose of waste as the rules require.

workedExamples.situation: A ceiling is being rolled, and the roller strokes leave overlapping lines when the light falls across the ceiling.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the likely cause, and what should the worker do?
workedExamples.reasoning: The likely cause is that the edge dried before the next section was rolled, or that the roller was pressed too hard and forced paint out in patches. Stop, check the load on the roller and the pressure being applied, and work in shorter sections so the wet edge is kept. Check the ceiling under a raking light, and correct the overlapping lines while the paint is still wet if the product allows it. If the lines have set, record them and check the data sheet before recoating.

workedExamples.situation: A cut-in along a window frame shows a clear dark band where it meets the wall, and the brush marks are visible along the edge.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Was the brush loaded correctly, and what should change?
workedExamples.reasoning: The band and the brush marks usually point to an overloaded brush, too much paint at the edge, or an edge that was worked for too long after the paint had begun to set. Next time, load the brush lightly, wipe off the excess, and cut in with a steady stroke in a shorter section. Keep the roller close behind the cut-in so the two blend while wet. Correct the current edge while the paint is wet, if the product allows, and record the correction.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a thicker coat to be rolled on a wall, saying that the first coat is patchy and they want it done in one go.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should you press harder and roll a heavier coat?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Pressing harder or loading the roller more heavily to get a heavier coat tends to cause runs, sags and uneven film, and it can go beyond what the product's data sheet allows. Check the data sheet for the film thickness and the number of coats the system needs, explain to the client that the patchiness is usually a sign of an under-loaded roller or a dry edge, and apply the number of coats the system calls for, at the rate the data sheet gives.

equipmentAndPpe: Brushes suited to the paint system, including an angled brush for cutting in
Rollers and sleeves with a nap suited to the surface texture
Roller tray, roller frame and extension pole
Drop sheets, masking tape and edging tools
Torch or work light for raking light inspection
Stable ladder or platform suited to the task
Eye protection and gloves suitable for the paint and cleaner
Respiratory protection where the product's data sheet or the site's assessment requires it, with a fit check

commonErrors.error: Pressing the roller hard to finish faster.
commonErrors.prevention: Use light pressure and let the roller carry the paint. Work out the pace from the wet edge, not from pressure.

commonErrors.error: Letting the edge dry before the next section is blended.
commonErrors.prevention: Work in shorter sections and keep a wet edge between them.

commonErrors.error: Overloading the brush at the edges.
commonErrors.prevention: Load the brush lightly and wipe off the excess before it touches the surface.

commonErrors.error: Going back over a mark once it has started to dry.
commonErrors.prevention: Correct while wet, and record anything that cannot be corrected.

commonErrors.error: Using the wrong sleeve for the surface texture.
commonErrors.prevention: Match the nap to the surface and check the result on a test patch.

commonErrors.error: Judging the finish under the light you are working in.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect under a raking light held low across the surface.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The licence test is set by the value of the work, not by the technique used to apply paint. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork have not needed one since 2015 unless the paintwork is part of other home building work. Other states are set out in “Paint systems, primers and coverage” and “Painting quotes, variations and colour approval”.
Solvent-based products and their rags: follow the product's safety data sheet for ventilation, ignition control and waste. Do not leave solvent-soaked rags in a pile.
Completing this lesson does not give a painting licence, certificate or authority to undertake regulated building work.

qualityStandard: Edges and corners are cut in cleanly, with no lap marks, under raking light.
The finish is even under a raking light, with no runs, roller stipple or missed spots left uncorrected.
Each section is blended into the previous one while wet, with no visible dry edge.
documentationEvidence: Finish inspection record made under raking light, with the room, the surfaces inspected, the time and the inspector's name.
Record of any defect corrected during the work, with the method used.
Record of any defect left open, with the reason and the agreed next step.
Photographs of the finish under raking light, taken with the client's permission (this consent rule is not confirmed by an official source).
summary: Cut in with a lightly loaded brush, and keep each cut-in wet until the roller blends it.
Roll with light pressure in a W or M pattern, and finish in one direction from the wet edge.
Inspect under a raking light and correct runs and lap marks while the paint is still workable.

knowledgeChecks.question: Roller marks appear on a ceiling where the edge has dried. What is the likely cause?
options: Too many coats on the ceiling surface
The room is too warm during the work
The wet edge was lost between sections
The roller is too new and has no nap

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best way to finish a rolled wall?
options: Press hard in circles to work the paint in
Leave the roller strokes showing on the wall
Roll only in the corners and skip the middle
Roll out in one direction with light pressure

knowledgeChecks.question: A dark band and brush marks appear along a cut-in. What is the most likely cause?
options: The colour is too dark for the room and needs a lighter coat
The brush was overloaded or the edge was worked too long
The ceiling was painted last, after the walls were done

knowledgeChecks.question: Which light best shows runs, lap marks and roller stipple?
options: A raking light held low across the surface
Direct overhead light only, from the fitting
No light, judged by touch alone along the wall
